items.stem: Which treaty defines who is a refugee in international law?
items.answer: The 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees
items.markingKey: The 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. It was extended beyond Europe by the 1967 Protocol.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant.
items.answer: A refugee has a recognised well-founded fear of persecution and the right to international protection; an economic migrant moves mainly for work or a better income and has no such protection. In practice motives overlap.
items.markingKey: A refugee has a recognised well-founded fear of persecution and the right to international protection; an economic migrant moves mainly for work or a better income and has no such protection. In practice motives overlap. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Refugees stay in camps only briefly before going home." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many refugees live in camps or exile for decades; Malkki's refugees had been in Tanzania since 1972.
items.markingKey: Many refugees live in camps or exile for decades; Malkki's refugees had been in Tanzania since 1972. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the bus station in Agadez, the drivers who take passengers north into the desert used to advertise openly. Since the 2015 law against migrant smuggling, they leave at night, without lights. Ibrahim, who once drove trucks of migrants to Libya, now sells phone credit. "Before, I was a transporter. Now they call me a trafficker," he says. A young man from Mali waits on a bench with a backpack and a plastic bottle wrapped in wet cloth. He has paid a "guide" whose name he does not know.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from Agadez, Niger.

Outline what the text reveals about how migration through the town has changed. Organise your answer as a series of clearly separated descriptive points.
items.answer: Drivers used to advertise openly but since the 2015 law they leave at night without lights; Ibrahim has gone from driving migrants to selling phone credit; he says he has been relabelled from "transporter" to "trafficker"; a young man from Mali waits with a backpack and wrapped water bottle, having paid an unnamed guide.
items.markingKey: Drivers used to advertise openly but since the 2015 law they leave at night without lights; Ibrahim has gone from driving migrants to selling phone credit; he says he has been relabelled from "transporter" to "trafficker"; a young man from Mali waits with a backpack and wrapped water bottle, having paid an unnamed guide. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Explain, with close reference to the text, how state power shapes migration in the text. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: A law (influenced by European pressure to externalise borders) criminalises a previously legal transport business, pushing movement into night-time, riskier routes and dependence on anonymous guides; classification changes Ibrahim's identity ("transporter" to "trafficker"); the border is effectively extended into the Sahara, increasing danger for migrants – comparable to Andersson's "illegality industry" and De León's Prevention Through Deterrence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A law (influenced by European pressure to externalise borders) criminalises a previously legal transport business, pushing movement into night-time, riskier routes and dependence on anonymous guides; classification changes Ibrahim's identity ("transporter" to "trafficker"); the border is effectively extended into the Sahara, increasing danger for migrants – comparable to Andersson's "illegality industry" and De León's Prevention Through Deterrence. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Identify one way in which identity matters in Andersson's Illegality, Inc. (along Spain's borders with Africa, including Ceuta, Melilla, Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal (fieldwork 2010–2012)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Migrants are categorised as "illegal" and learn to perform that identity or contest it in their dealings with officials and NGOs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Migrants are categorised as "illegal" and learn to perform that identity or contest it in their dealings with officials and NGOs. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Ruben Andersson, Illegality, Inc.: Clandestine Migration and the Business of Bordering Europe (2014), along Spain's borders with Africa, including Ceuta, Melilla, Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal (fieldwork 2010–2012)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Research with people engaged in now-illegal activities risks legal harm; the anthropologist must protect Ibrahim's identity, avoid recording routes or guides' details, and consider personal safety and the vulnerability of migrants. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Explain why participant observation is valuable in research on migration.
items.answer: Travelling, working and living with migrants (Holmes) reveals experiences of risk, labour and suffering that surveys or official statistics cannot capture.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Travelling, working and living with migrants (Holmes) reveals experiences of risk, labour and suffering that surveys or official statistics cannot capture. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why anthropologists criticise push–pull models of migration.
items.answer: They treat migrants as individuals responding mechanically to economic forces, ignoring kin networks, histories of colonialism and labour recruitment, state policies, aspirations and meanings that shape who moves and where.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They treat migrants as individuals responding mechanically to economic forces, ignoring kin networks, histories of colonialism and labour recruitment, state policies, aspirations and meanings that shape who moves and where. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Holmes's journey with Triqui migrants and explain what it reveals about labour migration and inequality.
items.answer: Holmes travelled with Triqui men from Oaxaca, crossed the border, worked on berry farms and was detained by the Border Patrol. Migration was driven by poverty linked to US agricultural policy and NAFTA, and migrants entered an ethnic labour hierarchy in the United States.
items.markingKey: Context (Holmes travelled with Triqui men from Oaxaca, crossed the border, worked on berry farms and was detained by the Border Patrol.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: migration was driven by poverty linked to US agricultural policy and NAFTA, and migrants entered an ethnic labour hierarchy in the United States. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to labour migration and inequality.

items.stem: "Migration is primarily an economic phenomenon." Discuss.
items.answer: Economics is central to much migration, but politics, violence, networks and meaning are equally important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: labour migration supplies workers to farms, factories and homes (Holmes); remittances support families. Arguments against: conflict and persecution force movement (Malkki); social networks, aspirations and identity shape migration; states and borders determine who can move. Supported judgement: Economics is central to much migration, but politics, violence, networks and meaning are equally important. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Who coined the term "social remittances"?
items.answer: Peggy Levitt
items.markingKey: Peggy Levitt. Levitt developed it from research on Miraflores and Boston.

items.stem: Briefly explain why transnationalism challenges older models of migration.
items.answer: Older models assumed migrants cut ties and assimilated; transnational research shows migrants living simultaneously in two places, sending money and ideas home and participating in politics and family life across borders.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Older models assumed migrants cut ties and assimilated; transnational research shows migrants living simultaneously in two places, sending money and ideas home and participating in politics and family life across borders. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Remittances only benefit the families who receive them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Remittances fund community projects and shape local economies, but can also increase inequality between migrant and non-migrant households.
items.markingKey: Remittances fund community projects and shape local economies, but can also increase inequality between migrant and non-migrant households. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example the Why We Post project, explain the relevance of change to diaspora and transnationalism.
items.answer: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Daniel Miller and colleagues, How the World Changed Social Media (Why We Post project, 2016), in a comparative digital ethnography by nine anthropologists in nine field sites, including Brazil, Chile, England, India, Italy, Trinidad, Turkey and two sites in China); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to change. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Levitt's study of Miraflores and Boston shows social remittances.
items.answer: Women in Miraflores adopted new expectations of men sharing housework after seeing migrant relatives in Boston; hometown associations funded projects. Ideas flowed from Boston to the village, changing gender relations and community organisation.
items.markingKey: Context (Women in Miraflores adopted new expectations of men sharing housework after seeing migrant relatives in Boston; hometown associations funded projects.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: ideas flowed from Boston to the village, changing gender relations and community organisation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social remittances.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the village in Kerala, the new houses have two storeys, marble floors and gates painted gold. Locals call them "Gulf houses". Many stand empty for eleven months of the year while their owners work in Dubai and Doha. Leela, whose husband has worked in Qatar for fifteen years, manages the money, the children's schooling and the land. "In the beginning I asked his mother for everything," she says. "Now the bank knows my name." When her husband returns each summer, he asks her how to pay the electricity bill online.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Kerala, India.

With reference to change, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Levitt's The Transnational Villagers. Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: Remittances transform the material landscape (Gulf houses as status symbols), while the husband's long absence shifts authority to Leela: she gains financial autonomy, independence from her mother-in-law and new competences, reversing knowledge roles with her husband – an example of migration reorganising households and gender relations transnationally. Ethnography – Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001), among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston: "Social remittances" – ideas, behaviours and identities – flowed from Boston to Miraflores, changing gender roles, politics and religious practice in the village. Comparison: similarities and differences in how change is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Define the term "social remittances".
items.answer: Peggy Levitt's term (1998) for the ideas, behaviours, identities and social capital that flow from migrant-receiving to migrant-sending communities

items.stem: Explain the difference between diaspora and transnational community.
items.answer: A diaspora emphasises dispersal from a homeland and collective memory, sometimes across generations; a transnational community emphasises current, active ties between specific places.
items.markingKey: A diaspora emphasises dispersal from a homeland and collective memory, sometimes across generations; a transnational community emphasises current, active ties between specific places. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Spain's two enclaves on the North African coast, whose fences feature in Andersson's Illegality, Inc., are:
options: Ceuta and Melilla
Calais and Dover
Gibraltar and Tangier
Lampedusa and Malta
items.answer: Ceuta and Melilla
items.markingKey: A. They are Spanish cities bordering Morocco.

items.stem: Explain the difference between cultural belonging and legal citizenship.
items.answer: Legal citizenship is formal membership of a state with rights; cultural belonging is the feeling and recognition of being part of a community. People may have one without the other.
items.markingKey: Legal citizenship is formal membership of a state with rights; cultural belonging is the feeling and recognition of being part of a community. People may have one without the other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Borders only affect people at the moment they cross them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Border regimes shape everyday life long after crossing, through deportability, documents and fear (Holmes, De Genova).
items.markingKey: Border regimes shape everyday life long after crossing, through deportability, documents and fear (Holmes, De Genova). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example Andersson's Illegality, Inc., explain the relevance of power to borders, citizenship and the state's control of movement.
items.answer: Andersson describes an "illegality industry" in which border police, contractors, aid agencies and media profit from controlling migration and help produce the "illegal migrant" they target.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Andersson describes an "illegality industry" in which border police, contractors, aid agencies and media profit from controlling migration and help produce the "illegal migrant" they target. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

On the bridge between the two towns, the queue for the border checkpoint stretches for a kilometre each morning. Women carry bundles of second-hand clothes on their backs; they are allowed to cross with "personal luggage" but not commercial goods, so each bundle is weighed to look personal. Rachida has crossed four days a week for eleven years. "The guards know my face, but every morning they look at my card as if I am new." Her son, born on the other side, has a passport; she does not.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a border crossing in North Africa.

Identify and describe how Rachida and the other women cross the border. Refer closely to the text. Write in your own words and keep close to the evidence in the extract.
items.answer: A one-kilometre queue forms each morning; women carry bundles of second-hand clothes, weighed to look like "personal luggage" rather than commercial goods; Rachida has crossed four days a week for eleven years; guards check her card every morning; her son has a passport but she does not.

Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that citizenship is the most important basis of belonging? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Citizenship is a crucial legal basis of belonging, but belonging also rests on community, identity and recognition.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: citizenship grants rights and security; statelessness is extreme exclusion; people belong to communities, diasporas and Indigenous nations beyond the state (Simpson); citizens may still be excluded by race or class. Suitable ethnographies include De León's The Land of Open Graves, Andersson's Illegality, Inc., Ong's Flexible Citizenship. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Citizenship is a crucial legal basis of belonging, but belonging also rests on community, identity and recognition. sovereignty
border
citizenship
items.answer: citizenship
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of citizenship.

items.stem: Explain why Indigenous nations may refuse citizenship of settler states.
items.answer: Accepting citizenship can imply accepting the state's sovereignty over their land; refusal (Simpson) asserts their own nationhood and continuing political existence.

Rachida has crossed four days a week for eleven years. "The guards know my face, but every morning they look at my card as if I am new." Her son, born on the other side, has a passport; she does not.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the border shapes Rachida's life and belonging. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: The border is a daily social process: rules about personal versus commercial goods produce informal livelihoods and tactics (weighing bundles); repeated checks show state power and the refusal to recognise her despite familiarity; citizenship divides the family (son with passport, Rachida without), so belonging and mobility are unequal even within one household.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The border is a daily social process: rules about personal versus commercial goods produce informal livelihoods and tactics (weighing bundles); repeated checks show state power and the refusal to recognise her despite familiarity; citizenship divides the family (son with passport, Rachida without), so belonging and mobility are unequal even within one household. items.stem: Briefly describe Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus and explain what it reveals about citizenship, sovereignty and refusal.
items.answer: Kahnawà:ke Mohawks refused Canadian and US citizenship and asserted Haudenosaunee sovereignty across the border. Their refusal shows belonging defined against settler states and borders imposed on Indigenous land.
items.markingKey: Context (Kahnawà:ke Mohawks refused Canadian and US citizenship and asserted Haudenosaunee sovereignty across the border.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: their refusal shows belonging defined against settler states and borders imposed on Indigenous land. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to citizenship, sovereignty and refusal.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Movement caused by conflict, persecution, disaster, development projects or other threats, rather than by choice"?
options: forced migration
push and pull factors
labour migration
deportability
items.answer: forced migration
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of forced migration.

items.stem: Aihwa Ong's Flexible Citizenship describes "astronaut" families in which:
options: children are sent to boarding schools in China
mothers work as pilots
fathers commute across the Pacific while wives and children live abroad
families travel to space
items.answer: fathers commute across the Pacific while wives and children live abroad
items.markingKey: C. It concerns elite Hong Kong Chinese families.

items.stem: Define the term "citizenship".
items.answer: Legal membership of a state, granting rights such as residence, voting and protection, and also a form of belonging and identity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: legal membership of a state, granting rights such as residence, voting and protection, and also a form of belonging and identity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Migrants move simply because wages are higher elsewhere." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Wages matter, but networks, histories, state policies, aspirations and family strategies shape migration (Holmes, Levitt).
items.markingKey: Wages matter, but networks, histories, state policies, aspirations and family strategies shape migration (Holmes, Levitt). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why diasporas often have complex relationships with homelands.
items.answer: Diasporas may idealise a homeland, fund development or opposition politics, face suspicion from both host and home states, and develop new hybrid identities distinct from both.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Diasporas may idealise a homeland, fund development or opposition politics, face suspicion from both host and home states, and develop new hybrid identities distinct from both. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between legal citizenship and cultural belonging.
items.answer: Legal citizenship is formal membership of a state with rights; cultural belonging is the feeling and recognition of being part of a community. People may have one without the other.
items.markingKey: Legal citizenship is formal membership of a state with rights; cultural belonging is the feeling and recognition of being part of a community. People may have one without the other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between voluntary migration and forced migration.
items.answer: Voluntary migration is chosen, often for work, study or family; forced migration is compelled by conflict, persecution or disaster. Anthropologists stress a continuum of constrained choices.
items.markingKey: Voluntary migration is chosen, often for work, study or family; forced migration is compelled by conflict, persecution or disaster. Anthropologists stress a continuum of constrained choices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Migrants inevitably lose their connection with home over time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many maintain intense ties through remittances, visits, social media and politics (Levitt, Why We Post), though ties change across generations.
items.markingKey: Many maintain intense ties through remittances, visits, social media and politics (Levitt, Why We Post), though ties change across generations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Stronger border controls stop migration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Ethnographies show tighter controls often reroute migration into more dangerous paths and create smuggling markets rather than ending it (De León, Andersson).
items.markingKey: Ethnographies show tighter controls often reroute migration into more dangerous paths and create smuggling markets rather than ending it (De León, Andersson). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how De León's The Land of Open Graves illustrates the concept of space, place and time. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: He describes the desert as a "hybrid collectif" of humans, animals, heat, terrain and policy that together produce migrant deaths.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: He describes the desert as a "hybrid collectif" of humans, animals, heat, terrain and policy that together produce migrant deaths. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Jason De León, The Land of Open Graves: Living and Dying on the Migrant Trail (2015), on the US–Mexico border in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, through the Undocumented Migration Project); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to space, place and time. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example Levitt's The Transnational Villagers, explain the relevance of belonging to diaspora and transnationalism.
items.answer: Migrants belonged to two places at once, joining village development and politics from Boston.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Migrants belonged to two places at once, joining village development and politics from Boston. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001), among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to belonging. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Andersson's Illegality, Inc. (along Spain's borders with Africa, including Ceuta, Melilla, Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal (fieldwork 2010–2012)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: Andersson describes an "illegality industry" in which border police, contractors, aid agencies and media profit from controlling migration and help produce the "illegal migrant" they target.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Andersson describes an "illegality industry" in which border police, contractors, aid agencies and media profit from controlling migration and help produce the "illegal migrant" they target. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Ruben Andersson, Illegality, Inc.: Clandestine Migration and the Business of Bordering Europe (2014), along Spain's borders with Africa, including Ceuta, Melilla, Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal (fieldwork 2010–2012)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Outline one way in which De León's Undocumented Migration Project in the Sonoran Desert shows the effects of border policy on forced and labour migration.
items.answer: Researchers documented migrants' objects, bodies and stories along routes where hundreds died each year from heat and exhaustion. Prevention Through Deterrence shifted risk onto migrants and made death look natural, showing state power operating through the landscape.
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers documented migrants' objects, bodies and stories along routes where hundreds died each year from heat and exhaustion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Prevention Through Deterrence shifted risk onto migrants and made death look natural, showing state power operating through the landscape. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effects of border policy on forced and labour migration.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the village in Kerala, the new houses have two storeys, marble floors and gates painted gold. Locals call them "Gulf houses". Many stand empty for eleven months of the year while their owners work in Dubai and Doha. Leela, whose husband has worked in Qatar for fifteen years, manages the money, the children's schooling and the land. "In the beginning I asked his mother for everything," she says. "Now the bank knows my name." When her husband returns each summer, he asks her how to pay the electricity bill online.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Kerala, India.

Using evidence from the text, describe the effects of Gulf migration visible in the village. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: Large two-storey "Gulf houses" with marble floors and gold gates; many stand empty most of the year; Leela manages money, schooling and land while her husband works in Qatar; she no longer depends on her mother-in-law; the bank knows her name; her husband now asks her about online bill payment.
items.markingKey: Large two-storey "Gulf houses" with marble floors and gold gates; many stand empty most of the year; Leela manages money, schooling and land while her husband works in Qatar; she no longer depends on her mother-in-law; the bank knows her name; her husband now asks her about online bill payment. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Using Andersson's Illegality, Inc. as an example, explain externalisation and the business of borders.
items.answer: Spain and the EU funded patrols, detention centres and deportation agreements with Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal, and media and NGOs became part of a border "industry". The border was pushed into Africa and controlling migration became an economy that reproduced migrant "illegality".
items.markingKey: Context (Spain and the EU funded patrols, detention centres and deportation agreements with Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal, and media and NGOs became part of a border "industry".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the border was pushed into Africa and controlling migration became an economy that reproduced migrant "illegality". – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to externalisation and the business of borders.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the bus station in Agadez, the drivers who take passengers north into the desert used to advertise openly. Since the 2015 law against migrant smuggling, they leave at night, without lights. Ibrahim, who once drove trucks of migrants to Libya, now sells phone credit. "Before, I was a transporter. Now they call me a trafficker," he says. A young man from Mali waits on a bench with a backpack and a plastic bottle wrapped in wet cloth. He has paid a "guide" whose name he does not know.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from Agadez, Niger.

Explain how state power shapes migration in the text, using one or more anthropological concepts. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: A law (influenced by European pressure to externalise borders) criminalises a previously legal transport business, pushing movement into night-time, riskier routes and dependence on anonymous guides; classification changes Ibrahim's identity ("transporter" to "trafficker"); the border is effectively extended into the Sahara, increasing danger for migrants – comparable to Andersson's "illegality industry" and De León's Prevention Through Deterrence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A law (influenced by European pressure to externalise borders) criminalises a previously legal transport business, pushing movement into night-time, riskier routes and dependence on anonymous guides; classification changes Ibrahim's identity ("transporter" to "trafficker"); the border is effectively extended into the Sahara, increasing danger for migrants – comparable to Andersson's "illegality industry" and De León's Prevention Through Deterrence. items.stem: "Transnational migrants belong fully to neither their home nor their host society." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Transnationalism produces multiple and sometimes conflicting belongings rather than an absence of belonging.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: migrants may face exclusion in both places; second generations may feel "in between"; many belong to both simultaneously (Levitt); transnational social fields create new forms of belonging. Suitable ethnographies include Levitt's The Transnational Villagers, Ong's Flexible Citizenship, the Why We Post project. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Transnationalism produces multiple and sometimes conflicting belongings rather than an absence of belonging. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Citizenship is the most important basis of belonging."
items.answer: Citizenship is a crucial legal basis of belonging, but belonging also rests on community, identity and recognition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: citizenship grants rights and security; statelessness is extreme exclusion. Arguments against: people belong to communities, diasporas and Indigenous nations beyond the state (Simpson); citizens may still be excluded by race or class. Supported judgement: Citizenship is a crucial legal basis of belonging, but belonging also rests on community, identity and recognition. items.stem: "Space, place and time is central to understanding labour migration, refugee flight and forced movement." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies and Agier's Managing the Undesirables, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies (with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005)): Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border with Triqui companions and was detained by the Border Patrol, showing how the border distributes risk unequally between bodies. Agier's Managing the Undesirables (based on fieldwork in refugee camps in Africa, including Kenya, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Zambia): Agier describes camps as spaces of exception and long waiting, separated from the national space around them, where temporary shelter becomes semi-permanent. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far space, place and time is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.
items.answer: Household finances and marital relations are private; Leela's comments about her mother-in-law and husband could cause family tension; anonymity of the village and family is needed. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "labour migration"?
options: The extension of border control beyond a state's territory, for example through agreements with transit countries
The supreme authority of a state or people over a territory, which Indigenous nations may assert against settler states
Movement of people, within or across borders, in search of work, often temporary or circular
Peggy Levitt's term (1998) for the ideas, behaviours, identities and social capital that flow from migrant-receiving to migrant-sending communities
items.answer: Movement of people, within or across borders, in search of work, often temporary or circular
items.markingKey: C. "labour migration" is movement of people, within or across borders, in search of work, often temporary or circular.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "diaspora"?
options: The supreme authority of a state or people over a territory, which Indigenous nations may assert against settler states
Someone forced to flee their home who remains within their own country's borders

Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a person outside their country who has a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion
A population dispersed from an original homeland that maintains a collective memory, identity and often an orientation towards that homeland
items.answer: A population dispersed from an original homeland that maintains a collective memory, identity and often an orientation towards that homeland
items.markingKey: D. "diaspora" is a population dispersed from an original homeland that maintains a collective memory, identity and often an orientation towards that homeland.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deportability"?
options: The supreme authority of a state or people over a territory, which Indigenous nations may assert against settler states
A population dispersed from an original homeland that maintains a collective memory, identity and often an orientation towards that homeland
Nicholas De Genova's term (2002) for the constant possibility of deportation that shapes undocumented migrants' lives and makes their labour cheap and disciplined
Movement caused by conflict, persecution, disaster, development projects or other threats, rather than by choice
items.answer: Nicholas De Genova's term (2002) for the constant possibility of deportation that shapes undocumented migrants' lives and makes their labour cheap and disciplined
items.markingKey: C. "deportability" is Nicholas De Genova's term (2002) for the constant possibility of deportation that shapes undocumented migrants' lives and makes their labour cheap and disciplined.

items.stem: Explain the difference between social remittances and remittances.
items.answer: Remittances are flows of money and goods; social remittances are flows of ideas, practices and identities. Both travel between migrants and home communities.
items.markingKey: Remittances are flows of money and goods; social remittances are flows of ideas, practices and identities. Both travel between migrants and home communities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists study borders as social processes rather than lines on a map.
items.answer: Borders are enacted through laws, patrols, paperwork, technologies and everyday encounters, and they shape lives far from the line itself (in workplaces, hospitals, schools), as De León and Andersson show.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Refugees stay in camps only briefly before going home." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many refugees live in camps or exile for decades; Malkki's refugees had been in Tanzania since 1972.
items.markingKey: Many refugees live in camps or exile for decades; Malkki's refugees had been in Tanzania since 1972. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between diaspora and transnational community.
items.answer: A diaspora emphasises dispersal from a homeland and collective memory, sometimes across generations; a transnational community emphasises current, active ties between specific places.
items.markingKey: A diaspora emphasises dispersal from a homeland and collective memory, sometimes across generations; a transnational community emphasises current, active ties between specific places. items.stem: Explain the difference between a frontier and a border.
items.answer: A border is a defined line of state jurisdiction; a frontier is a zone of expansion or contact where control is incomplete, such as Tsing's resource frontier.
items.markingKey: A border is a defined line of state jurisdiction; a frontier is a zone of expansion or contact where control is incomplete, such as Tsing's resource frontier. items.stem: With reference to Michel Agier, Managing the Undesirables: Refugee Camps and Humanitarian Government (2011), explain how the key concept of power helps us to understand labour migration, refugee flight and forced movement.

items.stem: "Change is central to understanding diaspora and transnationalism." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Levitt's The Transnational Villagers and the Why We Post project, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Levitt's The Transnational Villagers (among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston): "Social remittances" – ideas, behaviours and identities – flowed from Boston to Miraflores, changing gender roles, politics and religious practice in the village. the Why We Post project (in a comparative digital ethnography by nine anthropologists in nine field sites, including Brazil, Chile, England, India, Italy, Trinidad, Turkey and two sites in China): Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far change is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

On the bridge between the two towns, the queue for the border checkpoint stretches for a kilometre each morning. Women carry bundles of second-hand clothes on their backs; they are allowed to cross with "personal luggage" but not commercial goods, so each bundle is weighed to look personal. Rachida has crossed four days a week for eleven years. "The guards know my face, but every morning they look at my card as if I am new." Her son, born on the other side, has a passport; she does not.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a border crossing in North Africa.

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: Women engaged in informal cross-border trade risk confiscation or bans; photographs and names must not be published; the anthropologist should avoid detailing tactics that could be used against them. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that legal categories such as 'refugee' and 'migrant' help more than they harm? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Legal categories protect some people but exclude and stigmatise others; anthropologists study their effects critically.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: refugee status gives protection and rights; categories allow organisations to provide aid; categories exclude people with mixed motives; labels can stigmatise and fix identities (Malkki, Andersson). Suitable ethnographies include Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies, De León's The Land of Open Graves, Malkki's Purity and Exile. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Legal categories protect some people but exclude and stigmatise others; anthropologists study their effects critically. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "Remittances are the most important impact of migration on sending communities." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Financial remittances are important, but social and demographic effects may be more transformative.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remittances fund houses, education and health; they can be larger than foreign aid. Arguments against: social remittances transform ideas and practices; absence of migrants changes care, gender and politics. Supported judgement: Financial remittances are important, but social and demographic effects may be more transformative. Markbands (15 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.
